planting.note: Pre-sprout rhizome pieces indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, then transplant outdoors once soil is consistently warm and frost danger has passed. 'Bubba Blue' is distinguished from common culinary ginger by the blue-tinged coloring at the base of its young shoots and pseudostems.

directions: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in dappled shade to part sun; keep evenly moist through the growing season. 'Bubba Blue' is a named culinary ginger cultivar grown in university variety trials alongside other named strains for rhizome yield and quality comparison, notable for the distinctive blue-purple blush at the base of its stems and buds, which distinguishes it visually from plain commercial ginger while producing rhizomes of comparable culinary quality. Harvest young 'baby' ginger in 4-5 months for a milder, less fibrous root, or allow foliage to yellow and die back for a fully mature, more pungent harvest. In zone 8-9, mulch heavily or lift and store rhizomes over winter.

planting.note: Pre-sprout rhizome pieces indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, then transplant outdoors once soil is consistently warm. 'Hawaiian Yellow' produces golden-skinned rhizomes with canary-yellow flesh and can be grown as a warm-season annual in cooler parts of its range.

directions: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in dappled shade to morning sun; hill soil up around the base as the plant grows, similar to potatoes, to encourage larger rhizome development. 'Hawaiian Yellow' is a distinct culinary ginger strain grown widely in Hawaii, prized for its thin brown skin covering bright golden-yellow flesh with a fuller, more pungent bite than typical grocery-store ginger. It can be harvested young in late summer for tender, mild 'stem ginger,' or left in the ground until foliage dies back in fall for fully mature, storable rhizomes. In zone 9, plants die back after frost but the rhizome survives if mulched; further north, treat as an annual or lift and store rhizomes indoors over winter.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes 2-3 inches deep in spring once soil has warmed above 65F, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun. 'Chiang Mai Pink' is the original named clone that founded Thailand's commercial Siam tulip industry and is prized for its uniform, deep-pink bracts with darker pink tips.

directions: Plant rhizomes 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun after the soil has warmed in spring. 'Chiang Mai Pink' is the historic selection said to have been brought out of the wild to Chiang Mai by a Buddhist monk, becoming the foundation clone for Thailand's cut-flower Siam tulip trade; it is valued over seed-grown types for its compact, uniform habit and consistently deep rose-pink bracts with darker pink tips surrounding small true flowers. Plants emerge from dormant rhizomes in late spring, bloom through summer, and die back to dormancy in fall. As a cut flower, blooms last two to three weeks in a vase. In zone 9-11, rhizomes can overwinter in the ground with mulch; in colder zones, lift and store dry rhizomes above 55F over winter.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tropical Bulbs

planting.note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed, pressing seed lightly into the soil surface; this sticky-leaved annual self-seeds readily once established, so allow a few seed heads to mature and drop if a return crop is wanted.

directions: Sow directly in lean, well-drained soil after last frost and thin seedlings to 8-12 in apart; established plants tolerate heat and drought and need little care beyond occasional weeding. The deeply cut, oak-leaf-shaped foliage is covered in sticky glandular hairs that release a strong, sweet, resinous fragrance when brushed or crushed, and the branching flower spikes dry to a feathery, chartreuse-to-rust plume prized in dried arrangements and sachets. Cut whole flowering stems just as the tiny green flowers open and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy spot to preserve both scent and form. Historically the aromatic tops were also dried and used in traditional remedies for coughs and chest congestion, though it is grown today mainly as a fragrance and dried-flower herb.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; give it room to reach its full upright, more tree-like form.

directions: Selected by plantsman John Fairey of Peckerwood Garden, 'Bubba' is a vigorous, upright desert willow clone that grows more tree-like and symmetrical than typical seed-grown desert willows, reaching 20-30 feet tall with a strongly excurrent canopy. It bears an especially heavy, near-continuous flush of fragrant, bubblegum-pink flowers marked with dark burgundy throats from late spring through fall, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies all season. Because it is a low-seeding clone propagated by cuttings, it produces fewer messy seed pods than open-pollinated desert willows while still tolerating the heat, drought, and alkaline soils of the Gulf South and Southwest.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this fast clone benefits from a bit more room than the species to spread its rounded canopy.

directions: Selected by horticulturist Warren Jones at Boyce Thompson Arboretum, this desert willow cultivar grows faster than most seedling trees, holds its narrow willow-like leaves later into winter, and puts on a profuse, showy display of light pink, orchid-like flowers through the summer heat. Like the species it thrives in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil with minimal supplemental water once established, making it a tough, low-maintenance flowering tree for hot, dry Gulf Coast landscapes. It attracts hummingbirds and butterflies over a long summer-to-fall bloom season.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; its narrower upright habit fits tighter garden spaces than seed-grown desert willows.

directions: Selected at Boyce Thompson Arboretum, 'Rio Salado' is a more compact, narrowly upright desert willow cultivar reaching roughly 12-18 feet tall and wide, making it a good fit for smaller courtyards and street-tree plantings where a full-size desert willow would sprawl too far. It produces bright purple-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers over a long bloom season and shares the species' extreme drought and heat tolerance, needing little water once established in the lean, alkaline soils typical of the Gulf Coast and Southwest.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; its compact size suits patios and small yards better than full-size desert willow trees.

directions: One of the smallest-growing named desert willow selections, 'Lucretia Hamilton' stays large-shrub-sized at roughly 9-18 feet rather than developing into a full tree, making it well suited to patios and smaller garden spaces. It is prized for its saturated, deep magenta-burgundy flowers, richer in color than the pale pink of typical seedling desert willows, produced in a long summer-into-fall flush that draws hummingbirds. Like other desert willow selections, it wants lean, alkaline, sharply drained soil and full sun, and needs little supplemental irrigation once established.

planting.note: Set out container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; this cultivar is more tender than the species, so give it a protected spot or grow it in a container in zone 7-8 gardens.

directions: A striking sport of anise sage discovered with bright golden-yellow leaf margins surrounding rich green centers, 'Omaha Gold' pairs its variegated foliage with the same deep cobalt-blue, black-calyxed flowers that make Salvia guaranitica such a hummingbird favorite. It is more tender and slightly less vigorous than green-leaved forms, performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the gold variegation from scorching, and appreciates being grown as a container specimen in a protected spot where winters dip below zone 8. Because it does not come true from seed, propagate only from stem cuttings taken in summer. Pinch young plants to encourage bushier growth and more flowering side shoots.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once frost danger has passed, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to reach its full 8-foot spread by fall.

directions: Originally introduced as a hybrid but since determined to be a form of Cestrum parqui, 'Orange Peel' is a fast-growing, dieback shrub bearing terminal clusters of mustard-orange flowers tipped in yellow from early summer until frost, a color break from the greenish-yellow blooms of the straight species. It draws bees, hummingbirds, and other pollinators over a long season and tolerates sun to light shade with average to regular water. In colder winters within its range it dies back to the ground like other willow-leaved jessamines but returns vigorously in spring to reach roughly 8 feet tall and wide by fall.

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; unlike most rain lilies it is a single spring bloomer rather than a repeat-flowering summer species.

directions: Native to the eastern Sierra Madre of Mexico, Lindley's rain lily produces broad, glaucous, almost Hippeastrum-like leaves and soft pink, goblet-shaped flowers on 8-inch stems for a single flush from late April into May rather than repeating after every summer rain like most Zephyranthes. It is extremely drought tolerant and goes fully dormant in dry weather, with foliage returning only after rains resume, so gardeners should withhold summer irrigation once the spring bloom fades. Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light part shade, since standing moisture during dormancy is the main cause of bulb rot. Established clumps are long-lived and slowly offset into showy spring drifts well suited to rock gardens and dry borders.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in consistently moist, humus-rich soil to mimic the shallow, swift-flowing river shoals of the Cahaba, Flint, and Catawba river systems where it grows wild; a pond margin or boggy low spot works well in home gardens.

directions: Known as the Cahaba lily or shoals spider lily, this rare Southeastern endemic grows wild wedged into rock cracks on swift, shallow river shoals in Alabama, Georgia, and South Carolina, yet it adapts surprisingly well to ordinary moist garden conditions despite that specialized habitat. Strap-shaped leaves give rise in early summer to 18-24 inch stalks topped with clusters of intensely fragrant, white, spider-form flowers with six narrow whiskers extending past the central cup. It grows readily from seed and prefers a consistently damp to boggy site in full sun, such as a pond margin, rain garden, or low spot that never fully dries out. Because wild populations are vulnerable to damming and habitat loss, gardeners should buy nursery-propagated bulbs or seed-grown plants rather than wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, siting them permanently from the start since Baptisia forms a deep taproot and resents being moved or divided once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun and choose a permanent location, since Baptisia's deep taproot makes it a poor candidate for later transplanting or dividing. Bred by Tony Avent at Plant Delights Nursery from selections of Baptisia australis and Baptisia alba, Blue Towers grows in a distinctly narrow, upright, vase-shaped clump and sends up towering 18-to-20-inch flower spikes of periwinkle-to-lavender-blue blossoms in late spring, giving it far more vertical presence than typical false indigo cultivars. The blue-green foliage stays clean and attractive through summer, and the tall, dark seedpods that follow bloom provide movement and winter interest when left standing. Once established the plant is extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, needs only an annual late-winter cutback, and its foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies.
